The Quiet Return of the Night Train

By a staff writer

Sleeper trains were supposed to be finished. Cheap flights had taken their passengers, and by 2015 most of the old routes across the continent had closed.[1] Then something changed.

Dr. Elena Marsh, who studies transport at a small university, says the shift began with a simple sum: a night on a train costs about $89.50, and it replaces both a flight and a hotel room. "People did the maths," she said. "It isn't nostalgia. It's a bargain."

What the numbers say

Bookings on the busiest route grew 34% in a single year (see the operator's report at https://example.com/reports/night-trains-2024 for the full table). Three new lines opened, and two more are planned.

  • Trains leave after dinner and arrive before breakfast.
  • A private cabin sleeps two people.
const fare = 89.5;
console.log(fare * 2);

Not everyone is convinced. Critics point out that the carriages are old, the timetables are thin, and a single delay can strand a traveller far from home. Still, on a cold evening in the station, with the departure board flickering and a queue forming at the door of the sleeping car, it is hard not to feel that something worth keeping has come back.
